question: In the lecture\u2019s \u201cinteresting\u201d case, \(c\) is a cluster point of \(S\) and continuity at \(c\) is related to a limit statement. Contrast this with the \u201csilly\u201d case by analyzing the role of the interval around \(c\): explain why the existence of an interval \((c-\\delta_0,c+\\delta_0)\) containing no points of \(S\\setminus\\{c\\}\) removes the need for the \u201c\(0<|x-c|\u201d part that appears in the limit-style condition. Your answer should explicitly connect (a) the interval/intersection emptiness statement and (b) the two-case split \u201c\(x=c\) or \(x\\neq c\)\u201d used in the continuity proof when a limit hypothesis is assumed.
answer: If \((c-\\delta_0,c+\\delta_0)\\cap (S\\setminus\\{c\\})=\\emptyset\), then there are no \(x\\in S\) near \(c\) with \(x\\neq c\). So any condition that would normally require checking \(0<|x-c|<\\delta\) becomes vacuous: there are no such \(x\) to check. This is why the \u201cnear but not equal\u201d part (the \(0<|x-c|\) restriction) is unnecessary in the degenerate case. In contrast, when a limit hypothesis is used in the cluster-point case, the proof splits into \(x=c\) (giving \(0<\\epsilon\) immediately) and \(x\\neq c\) (where the limit hypothesis applies); the emptiness statement eliminates the \(x\\neq c\) branch entirely by forcing \(x=c\) whenever \(|x-c|<\\delta_0\).

\[
 f(x)=\frac{1}{3+\sin(x)^4}
\]
“makes perfectly good sense” for all \(x\) and hence can be concluded continuous by the algebraic theorem.

The constant \(3\) is used to assert “the bottom is always nonzero,” so the reciprocal step applies. Using only the facts that \\(|\\cos u|\\le 1\\) (from \\(\\sin^2 u+\\cos^2 u=1\\)) and \\(|\\sin t|\\le |t|\\), derive an explicit bound of the form \\(|\\sin x-\\sin c|\\le |x-c|\\). Explain why this bound is exactly what one needs to finish an \\(\\varepsilon\\)–\\(\\delta\\) continuity argument at \\(c\\).
answer:
Starting from \(\sin x-\sin c=2\sin\big(\tfrac{x-c}{2}\big)\cos\big(\tfrac{x+c}{2}\big)\), take absolute values:
\[
|\sin x-\sin c|=2\,\big|\sin\big(\tfrac{x-c}{2}\big)\big|\,\big|\cos\big(\tfrac{x+c}{2}\big)\big|.
\]
Using \(|\cos u|\le 1\),
\[
|\sin x-\sin c|\le 2\,\big|\sin\big(\tfrac{x-c}{2}\big)\big|.
\]
Then apply \(|\sin t|\le |t|\) with \(t=\tfrac{x-c}{2}\):
\[
|\sin x-\sin c|\le 2\cdot \Big|\tfrac{x-c}{2}\Big|=|x-c|.
\]

Define \\(z(x)=\\cos x+i\\sin x\\). Using only \\(\\sin^2 x+\\cos^2 x=1\\) and the meaning of absolute value for the complex unit circle given in the lecture, justify that \\(z(x)\\) lies on the complex unit circle for every real \\(x\\).
answer:
Let \(z(x)=\cos x+i\sin x\). Its (complex) absolute value satisfies
\[
|z(x)|=\sqrt{(\cos x)^2+(\sin x)^2}.
\]
Using the unit-circle identity \(\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1\), we get \(|z(x)|=\sqrt{1}=1\). Since the complex unit circle is defined as the set of complex numbers whose absolute value equals \(1\), it follows that \(z(x)\) lies on the complex unit circle for every real \(x\).

answer:
One valid reconstruction is:

\[
\sin\Big(x_n+\tfrac{\pi}{2}\Big)\to \sin\Big(c+\tfrac{\pi}{2}\Big).
\]

\[
\cos x_n=\sin\Big(x_n+\tfrac{\pi}{2}\Big),\qquad \cos c=\sin\Big(c+\tfrac{\pi}{2}\Big).
\]
5) Substitute these into step (3) to conclude \(\cos x_n\to \cos c\).

answer:

\[

\]

\[
\cos(x_n)=\sin(x_n+\pi/2)\to \sin(c+\pi/2)=\cos(c).
\]
Hence \(\cos(x_n)\to \cos(c)\).

question: In the lecture’s estimate of \\(\\left|\\int_a^b f_n-\\int_a^b f\\right|\\), the argument uses both absolute value and an inequality coming from uniform convergence. Explain why the lecture replaces \\(\\epsilon\\) by \\(\\epsilon/(b-a)\\) at a key step, and show how this choice forces \\(\\left|\\int_a^b f_n-\\int_a^b f\\right|<\\epsilon\\) for all \\(n\\ge m\\) using the triangle inequality for integrals.
answer:
Because integrating a uniform bound \(|f_n-f|<\delta\) over \([a,b]\) yields \(\int_a^b |f_n-f|\le \int_a^b \delta = \delta(b-a)\). To make the final bound equal to \(\epsilon\), the lecture chooses \(\delta=\epsilon/(b-a)\). Then for \(n\ge m\),
\[
\left|\int_a^b f_n-\int_a^b f\right|=\left|\int_a^b (f_n-f)\right|\le \int_a^b |f_n-f|\le \int_a^b \frac{\epsilon}{b-a}=\epsilon.
\]
The key tools are linearity (to write the difference as an integral of a difference) and the triangle inequality for integrals (to move the absolute value inside as an inequality).

question: In the lecture, a function \(f\) is defined as the limit of partial sums \(S_n(x)=\\sum_{j=1}^n f_j(x)\), and it is argued that \\(|f_j(x)|\\le m_j\\) for all \(x\) with \\(\\sum_{j=1}^\\infty m_j\\) convergent. Explain why the step \u201cchoose \(N\) so that \\(\\sum_{j=N+1}^\\infty m_j<\\epsilon\\)\u201d is enough to conclude that \(S_n\\to f\) uniformly (not just pointwise), and then state precisely what the uniform limit theorem lets you conclude about \(f\) given that each \(S_n\) is continuous.
answer:
Because \(\sum m_j\) converges, for any \(\epsilon>0\) there exists \(N\) such that the tail \(\sum_{j=N+1}^\infty m_j<\epsilon\). For any \(n\ge N\) and any \(x\),
\[
|f(x)-S_n(x)|=\left|\sum_{j=n+1}^\infty f_j(x)\right|\le \sum_{j=n+1}^\infty |f_j(x)|\le \sum_{j=n+1}^\infty m_j\le \sum_{j=N+1}^\infty m_j<\epsilon.
\]
The same \(N\) works for all \(x\), so the convergence is uniform. Since each \(S_n\) is a finite sum of continuous functions, each \(S_n\) is continuous; by the uniform limit theorem (uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous), \(f\) is continuous.

Using the lecture’s step “add and subtract \\(f_m(x)\\) and \\(f_m(c)\\) and use the triangle inequality,” explain how the choice of \\(m\\) coming from uniform convergence and the choice of \\(\\delta\\) coming from continuity of \\(f_m\\) combine to make each of the three absolute-value terms \\(<\\epsilon/3\\), and conclude \\(|f(x)-f(c)|<\\epsilon\\).
answer:
Pick \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) from uniform convergence so that for all \(y\in S\), \(|f_m(y)-f(y)|<\epsilon/3\). Then, since \(f_m\) is continuous at \(c\), choose \(\delta>0\) so that \(|x-c|<\delta\Rightarrow |f_m(x)-f_m(c)|<\epsilon/3\). For such \(x\), apply the triangle inequality after adding/subtracting \(f_m(x),f_m(c)\):
\[
|f(x)-f(c)|\le |f(x)-f_m(x)|+|f_m(x)-f_m(c)|+|f_m(c)-f(c)|.
\]
The first and third terms are each \(<\epsilon/3\) by the uniform bound (take \(y=x\) and \(y=c\)), and the middle term is \(<\epsilon/3\) by the choice of \(\delta\). Hence \(|f(x)-f(c)|<\epsilon\).

answer:
For any \(n\ge m\), the triangle inequality for integrals gives an inequality of the form
\[
\text{(integral of something involving }f_n-f\text{)}\le \int_a^b |f_n-f|.
\]
Once this reduction to \(\int_a^b |f_n-f|\) is made, the pointwise absolute-value bound \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|\le \epsilon\) (for all relevant \(x\), and in particular uniformly across the set once \(n\ge m\)) is the key input: it ensures the integrand \(|f_n-f|\) is everywhere bounded by \(\epsilon\), so the right-hand side integral is controlled for every \(n\ge m\).
